Bobby Gordon was born in 1942 in Hartford, Connecticut, and was raised on Long Island. He benefited from a close relationship with clarinetist Joe Marsala and he honed his own clarinet skills with Muggsy Spanier, Louis Armstrong and Wild Bill Davison after moving to Chicago. In the 60s and 70s, Bobby played with the Jim Cullum Band, Warren Vache and Max Kaminsky. He has performed with Leon Redbone, Keith Ingham, and Rebecca Kilgore, and he recently released “Bobby Gordon Plays Bing” on Arbors Records. He currently resides in San Diego.
Bobby was interviewed at the Allegheny Jazz Party in Chautauqua, New York on September 12, 1997 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe. We are interviewing today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive and it’s a pleasure to host Bobby Gordon, clarinetist. Welcome to Chautauqua.
You had a long flight from San Diego. How long have you been in San Diego?

I’ve been living in San Diego now for about the last seventeen years. I’m from New York City originally, and Long Island, Manhasset, Long Island, by way of New York City. And then I’ve been out in San Diego now for about seventeen years.
You can probably actually look at me which is okay. We have a camera right there too. What’s the West Coast jazz scene like in San Diego? Do you have to travel to play?

Well there’s a lot of festivals in California. There’s a festival every week if you really wanted to work that hard — all the way from San Diego I would say up to Seattle and Washington, Portland, Oregon, all the way across Utah, Nevada. You could work every weekend, you could play every weekend at a jazz festival if you wanted to, 52 weeks a year.

Well it depends on the type they are, and the type of bands that they have. Usually what I do is I travel, I make San Diego my base and I travel out of town, sort of do this type of a thing and things like that.
In the book we were just talking about, the recent jazz recording book, it describes you as a Dixieland, swing clarinetist. Is that a fair statement?
I would say that was very nice of them to say that. I’m proud of that, being a Dixieland and swing clarinet player.
